tldr: By running thousands of contact simulators in parallel on a GPU, this method selects the model that best explains recent robot motion online and uses it for CPU-based MPPI whole-body control, achieving rapid adaptation to unexpected payload shifts and leg failures without any offline training.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of the proposed LLA-MPPI framework. On the GPU side, numerous candidate simulators run to identify the best model from the most recent transition (Look-back). On the CPU side, MPPI samples control inputs using the chosen model (Look-ahead). Asynchronous decoupling of identification and planning is the key feature.
overview:
When legged robots operate in the physical world, discrepancies between the control model and real dynamics happen all the time. Payloads change abruptly, surfaces turn slick, and actuators can break down. Classical adaptive controllers force complex whole-body contact dynamics into simplified linear or point-mass representations, failing to capture frictional shifts or structural damage. Reinforcement learning (RL) with domain randomization offers robustness, but it remains brittle against out-of-distribution events and lacks physical interpretability.

To tackle this, the authors pursued an intuitive, brute-force concept: why not run thousands of parallel contact-rich physics simulations (MuJoCo Warp) on a GPU and select whichever simulator best reproduces the robot's recent motion on the fly? This is Look-back and Look-ahead Adaptive MPPI (LLA-MPPI). It uses a GPU-batched simulator bank to predict recent state transitions and rapidly pin down the best model, which is then fed to CPU-based MPPI (Model Predictive Path Integral) to optimize whole-body joint commands.

Across four challenging simulation tasks (asymmetric payload, leg lock, slope with low friction, and variable-mass box pushing), conventional adaptive baselines peaked at 74.0% success. LLA-MPPI achieved 97.5%, closely matching an ideal oracle with the true model (98.5%). Hardware tests on a Unitree Go2 quadruped demonstrated that the robot can handle mid-run payload additions, a disabled rear leg, and heavy box pushing without falling over.
contributions: A whole-body adaptive control framework that selects the best-matching model online from a GPU-batched bank of contact simulators, requiring no differentiability, affine structure, or explicit analytical equations.

A heterogeneous architecture that decouples GPU model identification (Look-back) from CPU MPPI trajectory optimization (Look-ahead) asynchronously, maintaining steady control latency regardless of bank size.
A sliding window and switching margin hysteresis mechanism tailored for legged systems to ensure stable identification despite intermittent contact and weak excitation.
A 97.5% success rate across four simulated tasks, along with hardware validation on a Unitree Go2 showing rapid adaptation to sudden payload shifts, leg locking, and variable-mass box pushing.

sections.heading: Why is adaptive control hard for legged robots, and how can GPU parallelism break through?
sections.summary: Legged robots frequently experience sudden changes in mass, surface friction, or actuator health. However, their contact-rich whole-body dynamics are non-smooth, breaking standard assumptions in adaptive control theory. This paper uses GPU-parallel simulation to bypass these mathematical roadblocks via direct model selection.
sections.details:
Real-time whole-body controllers (WBC) for legged robots have reached practical maturity, but they remain vulnerable to modeling mismatch. Existing solutions generally force a trade-off: either oversimplify the dynamics to apply classical adaptive control, or rely on offline reinforcement learning for implicit robustness.

### I-A Limitations of Prior Work
Classical adaptive control methods (such as model reference adaptive control, $\mathcal{L}_1$ adaptive control, and Kalman filtering) rely on strict assumptions: matched uncertainties, affine parameterizations, and persistent excitation (PE). Legged contact dynamics violate these conditions. As feet touch down and lift off, governing equations switch discontinuously. Consequently, standard methods struggle with physical changes like ground friction shifts or actuator failure.

Prior work has scaled Multiple Model Adaptive Control (MMAC) with GPU batching, but it was restricted to low-dimensional vehicle models. On the other hand, reinforcement learning (RL) degrades sharply outside its training distribution, and its latent representations lack physical interpretability.

### I-B Positioning and Contributions
To overcome these hurdles, this paper introduces LLA-MPPI. Instead of closed-form formulas, it runs an ensemble of contact simulators in parallel on MuJoCo Warp. The controller selects the model that minimizes prediction error against recent observations online. This allows a unified framework to handle everything from minor parametric drift to structural failures like lost limbs.

sections.heading: Formulating the problem: non-smooth contacts and sudden physical shifts
sections.summary: State transitions are non-smooth due to hybrid contact modes and can change abruptly mid-run. The problem is formulated as identifying the true physical model online from observed transitions using a predefined candidate model bank, while planning control trajectories that satisfy input bounds in real time.
sections.details:
Let the robot state be $\mathbf{x}_k=[\mathbf{q}_k^\top, \mathbf{v}_k^\top]^\top$ (generalized coordinates and velocities) and control inputs be target joint positions $\mathbf{u}_k \in [\mathbf{u}_{\min}, \mathbf{u}_{\max}]$ fed to low-level PD controllers. The transition mapping $f_k$ introduces two major hurdles inherent to legged locomotion.

First, contact conditions switch whenever feet or manipulated objects make or break contact, transitioning between stiction and sliding. Thus, $f_k$ is non-smooth and cannot be written in a single closed-form equation. Second, the mapping is unknown and can shift discontinuously during an episode due to payload drops or mechanical failures.

The system designer provides an offline candidate bank $\widetilde{f}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}; \bm{\theta})$ parameterized by $\bm{\theta} \in \Theta$, spanning anticipated physical and structural changes. Crucially, $\widetilde{f}$ can be a non-smooth contact simulator itself; linearity or differentiability with respect to $\bm{\theta}$ is never required.

At each time step $k$, the controller must determine the best hypothesis $\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_k$ from observed transitions and compute control inputs over a future horizon $H$ to minimize task cost $\ell$. Without access to gradients or convexity in contact dynamics, this optimization must run at millisecond-level real-time rates.

sections.heading: How it works: looking back to identify, looking ahead to plan
sections.summary: The system asynchronously pairs GPU-based 'Look-back'—replaying the last step across thousands of candidate simulators to pick the best model—with CPU-based 'Look-ahead' to optimize future trajectories via MPPI. A hysteresis mechanism prevents false switches during intermittent contacts.
sections.details:
### III-A Building the Physics Model Bank
The candidate model bank is built as $K$ parallel environments in MuJoCo Warp. The hypothesis set $\Theta_K$ is formed by taking the Cartesian product of continuous parameters (mass, friction) discretized into grids and discrete structural conditions (leg failure modes). These worlds are compiled into a single CUDA graph. Even with thousands or tens of thousands of candidates, a single kernel launch evaluates a one-step forward rollout across the entire bank.

### III-B Look-Back: Model Selection Under Intermittent Excitation
When the robot completes a real transition $(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k, \mathbf{x}_{k+1})$, all $K$ models simulate one step forward starting from $\mathbf{x}_k$. Prediction errors are computed for each model and averaged across a sliding window of the last $W$ steps. A key feature here is the switching margin $\gamma$. When legs are airborne, physical differences barely affect motion (weak excitation). To prevent noisy switching during these phases, the controller updates its model hypothesis only if a candidate beats the current selection by $\mathcal{E}_k^\star < \gamma \mathcal{E}_k^{i_{k-1}^\dagger}$ (with $\gamma \le 1$) for several consecutive steps.

### III-C Look-Ahead: Whole-body Trajectory Optimization via MPPI
Using the selected model $\widehat{\bm{\theta}}_k$, MPPI (Model Predictive Path Integral) on the CPU samples $N$ control trajectories in parallel over horizon $H$. Spline-smoothed Gaussian noise is added to the nominal trajectory, and rollouts are evaluated against tracking errors, PD torque penalties, and task-specific objectives like box positions. The nominal sequence is updated using a softmax-weighted average of costs, and the first command $\bm{\mu}_0$ is sent to the robot. Input bounds are strictly satisfied by clipping during sampling.

### III-D Decoupled Architecture: Splitting GPU and CPU
Look-back is 'wide and shallow' (evaluating many one-step simulations), making it an ideal fit for GPUs. Look-ahead is 'narrow and deep' (propagating fewer rollouts over multiple steps), which suits multithreaded CPUs. Decoupling the two asynchronously ensures that scaling the GPU bank to $K=10,000$ leaves the overall control loop time virtually unchanged at around 17.6 ms.

captions.F2: The LLA-MPPI system pipeline. On the GPU (top), the latest transition is simulated across all candidate models to identify the best fit. On the CPU (bottom), MPPI rollouts run on the selected model. Because identification is decoupled from the main planning loop, expanding the candidate bank does not penalize control frequency.

sections.heading: Benchmark results: robust simulation trials and real-world Go2 deployment
sections.summary: In four simulation benchmarks (asymmetric payload, leg lock, slope/friction, and box pushing), LLA-MPPI achieved a 97.5% success rate, outperforming adaptive baselines (42.5% for DOB, 74.0% for a particle filter). Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 confirmed stable recovery under sudden loads and leg disablement.
sections.details:
### IV-A Comparison with Model-based Adaptive Baselines
LLA-MPPI was benchmarked against a nominal fixed model (Nominal), a disturbance observer (DOB), continuous parameter estimation via a particle filter (CPE), and an ideal Oracle with true parameters. Across 50 trials per task (200 total), Nominal reached 25.5%, DOB reached 42.5%, and CPE achieved 74.0%. LLA-MPPI attained 97.5%, closely matching the Oracle's 98.5%.

- **Asymmetric payload**: A payload shifted laterally mid-walk. Using a bank of $100 \times 100 = 10,000$ hypotheses, the method quickly tracked center-of-mass shifts. On hardware, adding a 2.3 kg off-center weight caused Nominal to roll over, while LLA-MPPI restabilized and reached the goal.
- **Leg lock**: All joints in one leg froze mid-gait ($K=5$). Classical force-based disturbance observers fail under such topological shifts. LLA-MPPI detected the failure within three steps and transitioned into a three-legged gait. The Go2 robot maintained stable walking after losing its rear-left leg.
- **Slope and friction**: Terrain inclination and surface friction changed simultaneously ($10,000$ candidates). The controller accurately decoupled gravity shifts from foot slip.
- **Variable-mass box pushing**: The mass of a pushed box increased mid-run ($K=100$). On hardware, the robot rapidly increased pushing effort as mass was added and completed the task.

### IV-A Ablations: Window Length and Bank Size
Evaluating window length $W$ and bank size $K$ on the slope-friction task revealed a clear U-shaped curve for friction estimation error. Overly short windows succumbed to sensor noise, while overly long windows lagged behind rapid transitions. Error reached its minimum near $(K, W) = (257, 25)$, validating the chosen parameter $W=20$.

### IV-B Comparison with Domain-Randomized RL (PPO)
The framework was also evaluated against PPO trained for 200 million environment steps, with and without domain randomization. While RL is robust within its randomized range, heavy randomization often leads to overly conservative behaviors. In contrast, LLA-MPPI requires zero offline training time yet preserves agile, accurate tracking by identifying the exact dynamics online.

captions.F9: Ablation results on window length $W$ and bank size $K$ for the slope and friction task. Friction Mean Absolute Error (MAE) forms a U-shaped curve over $W$, degrading when the window is either too short or too long. The error is minimized at $(K, W) = (257, 25)$, marked by the star.

sections.heading: Takeaways and future directions: turning physics simulators into online estimators
sections.summary: LLA-MPPI demonstrates that running non-smooth contact simulators directly on a GPU enables whole-body adaptive control without mathematical smoothing or offline training. Future directions include dynamic grid refinement and uncertainty-aware multi-hypothesis planning.
sections.details:
This work establishes a powerful adaptive control paradigm enabled by GPU computing: using full physics simulators as explicit identification hypotheses. Even for non-differentiable contact mechanics, brute-force yet elegant model selection handles everything from parameter variations to limb loss within a unified structure.

However, the approach is inherently constrained by the predefined candidate bank, and identification is challenging when robot motions fail to excite underlying parameters. Looking ahead, the authors plan to explore adaptive bank refinement that subdivides promising parameter regions online, uncertainty-aware MPPI that plans over probability distributions of candidate models, and evaluations across more varied contact environments.

takeaways: With GPU physics engines like MuJoCo Warp, brute-force model selection across thousands of candidate simulations runs within milliseconds, making simulator-based identification practical.
Decoupling a wide-and-shallow GPU identification stage from a narrow-and-deep CPU MPPI planner keeps control loop times steady, even as candidate models scale up.
In systems with intermittent contact like legged robots, a sliding window and switching margin hysteresis are essential to prevent false model changes during low-excitation phases.
A structured physics model bank enables rapid online adaptation to hardware faults and mass changes without requiring massive offline reinforcement learning datasets.
limitations: The method cannot adapt to unexpected dynamics that fall completely outside its predefined candidate hypothesis bank.
When the robot does not sufficiently excite the dynamics (such as when feet are in the air), the controller cannot distinguish between candidate models and must stick with past hypotheses.
As the dimensionality of the parameter space grows, uniform grid-based discretization faces the curse of dimensionality, causing the required number of models $K$ to explode.
